item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Supreme court threatens midterms mail-in voting as it backs Trump plan | First Thing
item.description:
US president has been obsessed with restricting the ability to vote by mail, despite using it himself. Plus, why we are still fascinated with Meg from the White Stripes

  • Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here

Good morning. The US supreme court has sided with Donald Trump in his effort to crack down on mail-in voting, though it is unclear whether or not his administration will be able to take action before the midterm elections in November. The court’s justices voted 6-3 along ideological lines to lift an injunction that a judge in Massachusetts had placed in June on an executive order issued by the president. But a second injunction remains in place, and the ruling leaves room for legal challenges.

Trump has repeatedly likened voting by mail to cheating, despite his own use of it and overwhelming evidence that the system is secure. In March he ordered the government to create a “state citizenship list” of eligible voters, requiring that mail-in ballots only be delivered to people on that list. He also directed the justice department to prioritise investigations and prosecutions of state and local election officials who issue ballots to people deemed ineligible to vote in federal elections.

What did the dissenting judges say? In a blistering dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the decision “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections”.

How have rights organisations reacted? The president of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, Derrick Johnson, said: “Let this ruling be a reminder that democracy is never, ever guaranteed. We have to fight for it, we have to fight to keep it and we have to protect the rights we do have within it … they are trying to do everything they possibly can to make it difficult for you to vote.”

How has Canada reacted? The country’s prime minister, Mark Carney, told reporters that Trump’s announcement was largely expected. “It’s not a surprise for us that the US would take some form of reprisal to our response to their unjustified tariff,” he said. Carney has vowed to match the American tariffs “dollar for dollar”, and said Canada could not accept any proposed trade deal that would weaken French language protections.

ATT Monitor team, the body charged with overseeing the global Arms Trade Treaty, condemned on Tuesday a lack of transparency around states reporting the weapons they are buying and selling.

Adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 2013, the treaty aims to regulate the international flow of conventional weapons to stop their illicit trade.

While its 118 member states are supposed to submit annual reports on their weapons imports and exports, just 46 countries - less than 40 percent - submitted their 2025 reports on time, Alexandra Marksteiner, a member of the monitoring team, told a press conference in Geneva.

"The decline in meaningfully transparent reporting and publicly available information highlights larger issues around transparency in the global arms trade," the monitor said in a statement, adding that this is "particularly distressing in times of increasing military expenditure, escalating conflict and diminishing peace".

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan responded on Monday to Israeli strikes on a Syrian military base last week, saying Ankara would not abandon its friends in the region and that no outside power could set the boundaries of Turkish foreign policy.

Israel carried out several strikes on the Abu al-Duhur military airbase in northern Syria, approximately 70km from the Turkish border, claiming that Ankara was preparing to deploy air defence systems there.

Israeli officials have repeatedly said that the Turkish military's use of airbases in Syria would constitute a "red line," arguing that such a presence could restrict Israel's freedom of action in Syrian airspace.

Both Turkish and Syrian officials denied that Ankara had planned to deploy air defence systems at Abu al-Duhur, saying Turkish personnel were there solely to repair the runway and control tower. That account was also supported by US Ambassador Tom Barrack.

Erdogan, who had been on holiday for several days, notably refrained from mentioning Israel or Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu by name during his speech on Monday.

The Turkish Presidency said last week that the Israeli strikes were directly linked to Israel's elections in October, in which Netanyahu is expected to perform poorly.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Bangladesh could join Mecca pact, official suggests
item.description:
Bangladesh could join Mecca pact, official suggests

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 08/25/2026 - 17:03
According to Reuters, the consideration follows an invitation from Saudi Arabia
The military gathers as part of preparations for the election, at the National Stadium in Dhaka, Bangladesh on 5 February 2026 (AFP)
Off

Bangladesh may be joining the defence agreement signed by Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan earlier this month. 

Bangladeshi State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir told reporters on Monday that his country has been invited to participate in what has become known as the Mecca pact, but did not say who extended the invitation.

Reuters news agency, however, cited an unnamed source saying Riyadh had reached out to Dhaka. 

"If there is a security arrangement among Islamic nations in the Middle East, it is not unusual for us to consider participating. It is being viewed positively," Kabir said. 

The agreement stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three countries shall be regarded as an attack against all three, in a formula approaching the collective defence logic of major military alliances like Nato.

Bangladesh's participation would rock its regional standing as a country that tries to stay out of major geopolitical rifts, given it sits next to two nuclear-armed rivals in India and Pakistan.

However, it is still seeking the extradition of its former leader Sheikh Hasina, who fled to India in 2024 after mass protests toppled the government in Dhaka.

A Bangladeshi-Pakistani security alliance would likely be perceived as a threat to India, which maintains strong ties with Israel.

The Iran angle

The three countries in the Mecca pact have emphasised that it is defensive in nature and not directed against any particular state.

Many analysts, however, have suggested that the alliance between Ankara, Riyadh and Islamabad is targeted at Tehran.

The three states have largely Sunni populations, but while Saudi Arabia has had frosty relations with Iran, Turkey and Pakistan have remained relatively cordial with Tehran.

Islamabad has been a key conduit for negotiations between the US and Iran as they engage in a prolonged conflict over the Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has blockaded in response to the US and Israeli war on the country, which was initially aimed at toppling its government.

Saudi Arabia, on the other hand, has been the subject of Iranian retaliatory action primarily aimed at US military assets within its borders.

As the conflict has dragged on, hostilities have reignited between Saudi Arabia and its neighbours to the south, the Houthi-led administration in Sanaa, which controls most of northern Yemen.

Although Turkish officials initially envisioned a trilateral treaty, Middle East Eye was told that Egypt emerged as a natural candidate for inclusion in the mechanism.

Possessing a powerful military, Egypt increasingly found itself aligned with Turkey, Qatar and Saudi Arabia on issues ranging from the negotiations to end the war on Gaza to developments in Africa.

An Ankara-based source familiar with the discussions told MEE that Turkey had made considerable efforts to include Egypt in the treaty and had formally proposed its participation.

However, once it became clear that Cairo was not prepared to join, the other countries decided to proceed without it.

“America and other countries should know that the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened except through Iranian arrangements,” Gharibabadi said, adding that Iran remains “in a state of war”.

Gharibabadi says Iran and Oman have held talks over the past 40 days on a transit arrangement through the waterway, agreeing on a temporary route seven miles (11 kilometres) wide, with the entry point and part of the exit route running through Iranian territorial waters.

He said that activating the route agreed with Oman “means closing the southern route in the strait” that the US had opened “under pressure from Oman” - a move he said violated the US-Iran memorandum of understanding (MoU).

Gharibabadi said the proposed map for the route came from Iran’s armed forces, with negotiations on a permanent arrangement to follow, adding that the Iranian government had spoken to Pakistan, Oman and Qatar about these regional developments.

The warehouse belongs to Ard El Insan (AEI), a local humanitarian organisation working with MAP to support about 60 medical points serving up to 100 women and children daily.

The agreement stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three countries shall be regarded as an attack against all three, in a formula approaching the collective defence logic of major military alliances like Nato.

item.description:
Follow updates live

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Angela Jackson, the commissioner of the Productivity Commission, said the body stands by the interim report into the GST, which found the deal with Western Australia to be a costly mistake that should be reversed.

Jackson spoke to RN this morning after WA premier Roger Cook said “east coast clowns” didn’t understand the state and any changes would “rip $6bn out of the Western Australia economy”.

We are aiming, of course, to inform public policy debate, which can often get heated. Our view is that a line was crossed in terms of the nature of those comments from the Western Australian premier last month.

We welcome debate and we welcome criticism of our work and our report more broadly because it makes our work stronger. But to undermine and I guess attack our integrity, I think is an additional bridge too far. And I think something that more broadly we are seeing in public debate internationally.

It’s important for us to indicate that that process will not be influenced by the prime minister’s comments, that we are above politics, and that’s a very important position that we hold within the public policy landscape in Australia.
